title: Reactions to the war in the USA and Vietnam

review.note: Original content following 4HI1 Historical investigation A4, key topic 5.

learn.intro: The war devastated Vietnamese civilians and divided American society. Media coverage, the draft and events such as My Lai fuelled a growing protest movement, while many Americans continued to support the war.

sections.title: 1. The impact of the war on civilians in Vietnam

blocks.p: More bombs were dropped on Vietnam, Laos and Cambodia than by all sides in the Second World War. Villages were destroyed by search and destroy missions, napalm and bombing. Millions of Vietnamese became refugees, many moving into crowded camps and the slums of Saigon.

Agent Orange destroyed crops and forests and caused cancers and birth defects for decades afterwards. Estimates of Vietnamese deaths vary widely, but they run into the millions, many of them civilians.
Civilians were also caught between both sides: the Vietcong used terror against officials and those who helped the government, as in the killings in Hue during Tet in 1968.

sections.title: 2. Opposition to the war in the USA

blocks.p: The anti-war movement grew from 1965. Students held 'teach-ins' and marches; Students for a Democratic Society (SDS) organised protests. Young men burned their draft cards; the draft hit poorer and Black Americans hardest. Martin Luther King Jr spoke against the war in 1967, and the boxer Muhammad Ali refused the draft.

The media was crucial: Vietnam was the first 'television war'. Images such as the Saigon police chief executing a Vietcong prisoner during Tet (1968) and reports of My Lai (published November 1969) shocked the public.

Protest peaked in 1969–71: huge Moratorium demonstrations in October and November 1969; Kent State (May 1970); veterans throwing away their medals in 1971; and the Pentagon Papers (1971) revealing that governments had misled the public.

sections.title: 3. Support for the war and the legacy

blocks.p: Not all Americans opposed the war. Many saw it as a fight against communism and saw protesters as unpatriotic. Nixon appealed to the 'silent majority' in November 1969. In May 1970 construction workers attacked anti-war students in New York (the 'Hard Hat Riot').

The war's legacy in the USA: about 58,000 Americans died; veterans often returned to a hostile or indifferent reception and many suffered long-term trauma; Congress passed the War Powers Act (1973) to limit the President's power to wage war; and trust in government fell.

people.name: Martin Luther King Jr
people.role: Civil rights leader who opposed the war from 1967.

vocab.def: Nixon's term for Americans who quietly supported the war.

misconceptions.right: Many supported it; Nixon appealed to the 'silent majority'.

misconceptions.wrong: The protest movement was only students.
misconceptions.right: It included civil rights leaders, veterans, celebrities and many ordinary people.

mcq.q: Why is Vietnam called the first 'television war'?
options: It was filmed for films only
It was shown widely on TV news
It was broadcast live in Vietnam

mcq.q: What did the Pentagon Papers reveal?
options: That governments had misled the public about Vietnam
Americans who quietly supported the war

mcq.q: Which civil rights leader spoke out against the war in 1967?
mcq.why: He linked the war to poverty and racism.

mcq.q: What happened to millions of Vietnamese civilians?

short.q: About how many Americans died in the war?
In which year were the Pentagon Papers published?

matching.title: Match the event to its year

evidence.q: Give precise evidence of opposition to the war in the USA.
evidence.model: Millions joined the Moratorium protests in October–November 1969; four students were shot at Kent State in May 1970; the Pentagon Papers (1971) showed the public had been misled.

flashcards.q: Describe the impact of the war on Vietnamese civilians.
flashcards.a: Villages destroyed; millions of refugees; Agent Orange illnesses and birth defects; terror from both sides.

flashcards.q: Why did opposition grow in the USA?
flashcards.a: TV images, the draft, rising US casualties, My Lai, Kent State, the Pentagon Papers.

flashcards.q: Why did the draft cause anger?
flashcards.a: It hit poorer and Black Americans hardest; students could often defer.

flashcards.q: Give evidence of support for the war.
flashcards.a: Nixon's 'silent majority' speech (1969); the Hard Hat Riot (May 1970).

flashcards.q: What was the War Powers Act?
flashcards.a: A 1973 law limiting the President's power to send troops without Congress.

checklist.text: I can describe the impact of the war on civilians in Vietnam.
I can explain why opposition to the war grew in the USA.
I can judge how far American attitudes to the war changed.
